title: Joshua 24:29–33
context: Joshua the servant of the LORD dies at one hundred ten and is buried in his inheritance at Timnathserah; Israel serves the LORD throughout his lifetime and that of the elders who outlived him. Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem in the plot Jacob bought, and Eleazar son of Aaron dies and is buried in the hill country of Ephraim. Both traditions read these closing notices as shared ground: God’s promises fulfilled, faithful servants honored, and a generation’s faithfulness tied to remembering God’s works.

verses.text: After these things, Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being one hundred ten years old.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua son of Nun, “the servant of the LORD,” dies at one hundred ten years old. Arminian readers note that he receives the title earlier given to Moses (Deut 34:5).

His age matches Joseph’s at death (Gen 50:26), linking the two men buried in this closing passage.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Joshua honored as a faithful servant who finished his task.

Judges 2:8 repeats this notice. Joshua began as Moses’ assistant and ends with the same title of honor, a sign of God’s faithfulness through his life.

verses.text: They buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnathserah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north of the mountain of Gaash.
verses.arminianNotes:
They bury Joshua within his inheritance at Timnathserah in the hill country of Ephraim. Arminian readers note that this was the city he had asked for and received (Josh 19:50).

Judges 2:9 calls it Timnath Heres, a variant name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Joshua resting in the land God promised and gave.

The leader who distributed the inheritance is buried in his own share of it. The exact location is uncertain, so the notes do not try to identify it.

verses.text: Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, and had known all the work of the LORD, that he had worked for Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who had known the LORD’s work. Arminian readers note that faithfulness was tied to remembering God’s acts.

Judges 2:7, 10 tells of a later generation that did not know the LORD or his works.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the importance of testimony and memory in passing on faith.

The later generation’s failure (Judg 2:10) shows that each generation needs to know God for itself, which both traditions see as a call to faithful teaching.

verses.text: They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem, in the parcel of ground which Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of silver. They became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph’s bones, brought up from Egypt, are buried at Shechem in the land Jacob bought. Arminian readers note the fulfillment of Joseph’s request (Gen 50:25; Exod 13:19).

The WEB footnote explains the “pieces of silver” as kesitahs (cf. Gen 33:19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faith in God’s promise honored at last (Heb 11:22).

Acts 7:16 refers to a tomb at Shechem in wording that interpreters have discussed in relation to Genesis 23 and 33. The burial closes a story that began in Genesis.

verses.text: Eleazar the son of Aaron died. They buried him in the hill of Phinehas his son, which was given him in the hill country of Ephraim.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eleazar son of Aaron dies and is buried in the hill of Phinehas his son in Ephraim. Arminian readers note that the priestly line continues through Phinehas (Num 25:7–13).

The book ends with three burials in the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the passing of the first generation of leaders in the land.

The priesthood, like the leadership, continues to the next generation. Both traditions read these closing notices as a testimony to God’s faithfulness.
